cards.question: A server handles 100 req/s. Traffic spikes to 150 req/s for 60 seconds. How many requests are queued after the spike?
cards.key_concept: Queue depth = excess arrival rate × duration

cards.question: Same scenario: after the spike, traffic returns to exactly 100 req/s (the server's max capacity). How long to drain the queue?
cards.answer: Never. At 100% utilization there is zero spare capacity. The queue only drains if arrival rate drops BELOW max throughput. At 80 req/s → 20 req/s spare → 3000/20 = 150 seconds.
cards.key_concept: A system at 100% utilization has zero recovery capacity

cards.question: A server has 10 slots and 100ms service time. What is its throughput? What real-world things do 'slots' represent?
cards.answer: Throughput = slots × (1000/serviceMs) = 10 × 10 = 100 req/s. Slots represent parallel threads, connections, or workers (e.g., nginx worker_connections, PostgreSQL max_connections, Node.js thread pool size).
cards.key_concept: Throughput is derived from slots × service rate, not configured directly

cards.question: Server A: 10 slots / 100ms. Server B: 100 slots / 1000ms. Both do 100 req/s. Which is better for real-time chat? For batch pipelines? Why?
cards.answer: Chat: Server A — low per-request latency (100ms base) matters for real-time UX, though it's more fragile under bursts. Batch: Server B — high parallelism, latency doesn't matter, can process many items concurrently.
cards.key_concept: Same throughput can mean very different latency vs concurrency tradeoffs

cards.question: Why do production systems target ~70% utilization instead of maximizing to 100%?
cards.answer: The remaining ~30% is recovery headroom. At 100% utilization, any traffic spike causes permanent queue growth (no spare capacity to drain). The 30% buffer absorbs spikes and lets the system recover naturally.
cards.key_concept: Headroom = recovery capacity. No headroom = no recovery.

cards.question: State Little's Law and explain what each variable means in the context of a web server.
cards.answer: L = λ × W. L = average number of requests in the system (in-flight + queued). λ = arrival rate (req/s). W = average time a request spends in the system (service time + queue wait). As utilization → 100%, W → infinity, so L → infinity.
cards.key_concept: Little's Law connects queue depth, arrival rate, and latency

cards.question: 3 servers behind a load balancer at 250 req/s. One server's service time increases 5x (e.g., GC pause, bad disk). What happens to overall system latency and why?
cards.answer: Overall latency spikes dramatically. The LB still routes traffic to the slow server. With least-loaded routing, the slow server gets less traffic but doesn't get zero. Requests hitting it see huge latency. p99 spikes because ~some fraction of all requests still land on the degraded instance. Even healthy servers can't compensate — they can only serve their own traffic.
cards.key_concept: The slow server problem — one degraded instance poisons system-wide latency percentiles

cards.question: Your system is at 90% capacity. Clients retry failed requests 3 times with a 200ms timeout. A downstream service starts responding slowly (300ms). What happens and why?
cards.answer: Retry storm. Every request hitting the slow service times out at 200ms and retries 3 times. Original 100 req/s becomes up to 400 req/s of actual load. The system was already at 90% — the extra retries push it past 100%, causing more timeouts, causing more retries. Positive feedback loop → total collapse.
cards.key_concept: Retries multiply load. Under stress, they create a positive feedback loop that amplifies failure.

cards.question: You're on-call at 3am. p99 spiking everywhere, error rates climbing, you suspect a retry storm. What's your first action? What do you explicitly NOT do?
cards.answer: FIRST: Disable or reduce retries (config push, feature flag, set retry count to 0). This breaks the amplification loop — if 80% of traffic is retries, killing retries cuts load 80% instantly. Alternative: increase timeouts so healthy servers stop timing out. DO NOT: scale out (new servers fill instantly if retries multiply load 3-4x), restart services (cold = slower = more timeouts = worse storm), or deep-dive into root cause before stabilizing. Order: mitigate → stabilize → investigate → fix → postmortem.
cards.key_concept: The fastest way to end a retry storm is to stop retrying. Fix the amplification loop before adding capacity.

cards.question: Circuit breaker vs rate limiter: what does each protect, what triggers each, and when do you use which?
cards.answer: Circuit breaker: protects the CALLER from a broken dependency. Triggers on failure rate (errors/timeouts). Stops calling downstream entirely, fails fast, lets the broken service recover. Rate limiter: protects the SERVICE from too many callers. Triggers on request count. Rejects excess, keeps serving up to the limit. Breaker = 'dependency is sick, stop hitting it.' Limiter = 'I'm healthy but can only handle this much.'
cards.key_concept: Circuit breakers protect outward (stop calling broken things), rate limiters protect inward (stop being overwhelmed)
